Issued at 222 PM CST Wed Nov 25 2026

Through Friday Morning:

Late this afternoon, showery activity lifting north-
northwestward into a dry air mass with sub-freezing wet bulb 
temperatures will yield occasional flurries (possibly mixed 
with sprinkles). No accumulations and thus impacts are expected
with actual air temperatures well above freezing.

Tonight, phasing between negatively tilted trough/upper low over
the central US and a short-wave along the Gulf Coast will lead 
to the rapid strengthening and north-northwestward movement of 
a surface low pressure system from the Carolina coast toward the
central Appalachian Mountains. A broad and intensifying region 
of upper-level divergence within the merging waves will 
facilitate the continued expansion of an elongated north- 
northwest to south-southeast oriented deformation band from 
the lower Ohio Valley to the mid Mississippi Valley. 

Meanwhile, a steady feed of dry air into the Lower Great Lakes 
on the southern side of a retreating high pressure system should
impede the northward progress of the rain shield overnight, 
confining precip of note to primarily southwest of the local 
area. Continued northeasterly winds (onshore flow) and overcast 
skies will lead to a muted diurnal temperature drop tonight with
overnight lows favored to stay in the mid to upper 30s (around 
40F near the lakeshore).

On Thanksgiving Day through early Friday morning, the two 
upper-level waves will fully consolidate, pulling the surface 
low northward toward Lake Erie. A formidable northwestward push 
of the warm conveyor belt and associated column moisture in the 
mature cyclone during the afternoon hours should allow for an 
associated gradual northward push of the deformation rainfall 
band. Continued modest spread in the ensemble envelope on the 
exact track of the surface low still lends some uncertainty to 
the sharp northwestern edge of the precipitation shield. The
GFS/GEFS is farther southeast, while the remaining non-GFS
consensus is generally a bit farther northwest. 

Our forecast favors the northwestern edge of the steady rain 
making it to I-55 by early Thursday evening and then pivoting 
slowly northward towards southeast Wisconsin through the 
evening. Confidence is lowest with northwestward extent, and it
may remain mostly or completely dry in parts of our northwest 
CWA, including locations in and near Rockford. Steady rain will
then continue within the deformation band through the overnight
hours before tapering quickly from west to east into Friday 
morning.

The implied forecast surface pressure pattern features the
aforementioned deep surface low encroaching upon elongated high
pressure from eastern Canada to the north central US. This is
quite conducive to blustery northeast winds peaking Thursday 
afternoon through early Friday, strongest near the Lake Michigan
shore. Gusts will likely top out in the 30-35 mph range inland
of the lake and 35-45 mph along the immediate lakeshore. If the
farther northwest side of the guidance envelope with the 
surface low pressure track appears more likely to verify closer
to reality (than the GFS/GEFS), some consideration may need to
be given to wind advisory issuance for our lakeshore counties.

All in all, Thanksgiving afternoon and evening is shaping up to
be rather raw, particularly where steady rain overlaps with the
blustery northeast winds. Wind chill values for the drive home
from Thanksgiving dinner look to range from the upper 20s to mid
30s.

Friday Afternoon through Wednesday:

Upper level short-wave ridging will slide into the Great Lakes
Friday afternoon, bringing gradually clearing skies and highs
reaching the mid to locally upper 40s. An initial short-wave
passing to our north Friday night into Saturday may bring
spotty light precip to our north. Highs on Saturday will be
seasonably mild, in the upper 40s to lower 50s. Then on 
Saturday night into Sunday, a stronger short-wave and associated
surface low passing to our south will bring rain to at least 
parts of our area. Note that there should be a sharp cutoff 
once again on the northwestern edge of the precipitation shield.
In the wake of the weekend system, dry weather will return
through mid next week. Monday may be relatively cool (near to 
slightly above normal temps), followed by solidly above normal
temperatures Tuesday and Wednesday for the start of December
(and meteorological winter).

Castro/Borchardt
